analysis:
The PR changes three operator-facing diagnostics: DoctorRunner.swift (lines 37-38, 78-79), DoctorCommand.swift (358-361, 414-415) and StatusCommand.swift (135-140). Each now reads authorization through displayedProviderAuthorization(...), and also reads currentProviderAuthorization(...) as removalAuthorization. Both are passed to ProviderAuthorizationReadiness.summary(authorization, removalAuthorization:, now:).

All changes are read-only presentation of local daemon state. No network, wire, key, or authorization-grant logic is touched. The coordinator remains the authority for serving permission (T-052, T-053), and the daemon owns grant application and revocation. The CLI diagnostics do not feed back into any grant or revocation decision.

How the displayed value affects the operator: appAttestAuthorized is computed from the displayed authorization. That value controls the "serving authorization" pass/warn level and whether MDM/attestation-readiness hints are suppressed. If displayedProviderAuthorization can return an expired or revoked authorization that currentProviderAuthorization would reject, doctor could show a stale "authorized" pass. This is a diagnostic-accuracy concern only (T-058 overstated-trust framing), not an access-control bypass.

The passed removalAuthorization is meant to let summary() explain a removal or lapse. summary() receives the current-only value, so the lapse should still be surfaced. hasCurrentAppAttestAuthorization(now:) is still evaluated on the displayed value, so expiry is checked at display time.

Unverified: the implementations of displayedProviderAuthorization and ProviderAuthorizationReadiness.summary are not in the supplied evidence. Whether the displayed variant filters expired or revoked grants, and whether the summary text could misstate trust, cannot be confirmed. No concrete regression is identified from the supplied lines. The next pass should check those two ProviderCore definitions if the diagnostic's accuracy is considered security-relevant.
